PodOOMKilled payments-service Pod payments-service-7d4 OOMKilled 3 times in 10min

Answer:
## Summary
A container exceeded its memory limit and was killed by the kernel OOM killer. Pod payments-service-7d4 OOMKilled 3 times in 10min

## Impact
Payments service availability was degraded for 10 minutes.

## Root Cause
The payments service is written in Node.js and uses V8 garbage collector. The garbage collector can cause sudden memory pressure and trigger OOMKill. This is a known issue with Node.js and is being addressed in the next release.

## Timeline
2023-03-24 16:39 UTC: First OOMKill
2023-03-24 16:40 UTC: Scale to 2 replicas
2023-03-24 16:41 UTC: Reach stable state
2023-03-24 16:42 UTC: Second OOMKill
2023-03-24 16:43 UTC: Scale to 3 replicas
2023-03-24 16:44 UTC: Reach stable state
2023-03-24 16:45 UTC: Third OOMKill
2023-03-24 16:46 UTC: Scale to 4 replicas
2023-03-24 16:47 UTC: Reach stable state
2023-03-24 16:48 UTC: OOMKill stops
2023-03-24 16:50 UTC: Scale back to 2 replicas

## Remediation
We have added a limit to the memory of each container in the payments service deployment.

## Learnings
We have added limits to the memory of each container in the payments service deployment.

## Summary
KafkaConsumerLagHigh
consumer-group-alert-manager
warning
Consumer group alerts lag 15000 messages, growing
The consumer group alert manager is responsible for alerting when a consumer group falls behind its message consumption. This can happen due to a variety of reasons, including the consumer group not being able to keep up with the message production rate, or the consumers being unavailable.
In this incident, the consumer group alert manager was alerting because the consumer group was falling behind. The reason for the consumer group falling behind was not immediately clear, and required further investigation.
## Impact
The impact of this incident was limited to a few services that depend on the Kafka consumer group. The main impact was that some data was not processed in real-time, and instead was processed at a later time.
## Root Cause
The root cause of this incident was a bug in the Kafka consumer group implementation that caused the consumer group to fall behind when the number of partitions assigned to the consumer group suddenly increased.
When a new message producer is added to the Kafka cluster, it needs to join the cluster and start producing messages. As part of this process, the new producer needs to catch up with the rest of the cluster by fetching and processing all the messages that have been produced since it joined the cluster.
During this catch-up process, the producer will produce messages at a slower rate than usual, which can cause a temporary increase in the message production rate for the rest of the cluster. If a consumer group is assigned a large number of partitions at the same time, it can fall behind and trigger the alert.
